text.p: A U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit called to accelerate the battle against hunger ended on Sunday after five days of debate.

The summit, at the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) in Rome, adopted at its outset a declaration and plan of action in which countries pledged to halve the number of the world's hungry from 840 million people by no later than 2015.

"The dedication, commitment, will guarantee action...that all together we will work hand in hand to ensure that young children and babies will not cry of hunger and that mothers will not be looking at children who have no hope," FAO director-general Jacques Diouf told the closing session.
He was due to hold a final news conference with several leaders, including Cuban President Fidel Castro, at 1600 GMT.

The summit documents, which took more than two years to negotiate, are non-binding although Diouf said they were "the greatest indication that together we will win against poverty, we will win against scepticism".

But, in a sign that even compromise language had not resolved fundamental differences between rich and poor nations, Washington submitted written reservations on some items including the key issue of right to access to food. The United States was among 15 countries that raised reservations. Other delegations, including the Vatican, Argentina and several Moslem states, objected on population issues.
